candidates.attacker_control: The pod/container being copied from. Copy.java:124-130 runs sh -c "tar cz - <srcPath> | base64" inside that container and treats the resulting stream as trusted, so a malicious image, compromised container, or replaced tar/sh binary can emit a crafted tar with entry names containing '../' segments. No host-side constraint prevents it: Apache Commons Compress only parses names and the Java code performs the extraction itself, so tar's own extraction-time protections never run.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: (1) canReadEntryData(entry) (line 136) is a format check, not a traversal guard. (2) new File(parent, child) makes an absolute child relative to parent in java.io, so the practical vector is '..' segments, which are not filtered. (3) mkdirs() calls in the method do not constrain the path; they create the traversed directories. (4) The untrusted pod is inside the API's normal threat model because the client itself executes the container's tar via sh -c and the method's purpose is copying FROM a pod; Kubernetes treated the identical kubectl cp pattern as a vulnerability (CVE-2019-11246/11249) and fixed it with client-side tar path validation, which this implementation lacks. (5) I searched the whole class for canonicalization/sanitization helpers: none exist.
candidates.impact: Arbitrary relative file write/overwrite on the host running the client application, outside the caller-selected destination, within the JVM account's privileges. Depending on that account this enables overwriting configuration/credential/startup files, planting files in the user's home (for example ~/.ssh/authorized_keys, shell profiles, CI job configs) leading to code execution/persistence on the client host, and denial of service by clobbering files. The client host is the victim; the attacker only needs to control the copied-from container's tar output.
candidates.prerequisites: 1) The application calls Copy.copyDirectoryFromPod (the API itself requires exec access to the pod). 2) The source pod/container is attacker-influenced (multi-tenant cluster, user-supplied or third-party pod, compromised image, or a tool that copies from arbitrary pods). 3) The JVM user has write permission on the traversed target paths. isTarPresentInContainer() only checks that tar exists, not that the pod is trusted.
candidates.root_cause: The method extracts a tar archive whose bytes are fully controlled by the target container but never validates entry names: entry.getName() is used directly to build the output path (new File(destination.toFile(), entry.getName())), directories are created with mkdirs() and entry bytes are written with FileOutputStream, with no normalize()/getCanonicalPath() containment check and no rejection of '..' segments; canReadEntryData() (line 136) only checks archive/format readability. The archive is generated by running the container's own tar/sh/base64 (line 127), so the container controls the raw tar bytes, not merely its filesystem contents.
candidates.title: Path traversal (Zip Slip) in Copy.copyDirectoryFromPod lets a malicious pod write arbitrary files on the client host
candidates.trace: Copy.java:123-130 exec("sh","-c","tar cz - " + srcPath + " | base64") -> proc.getInputStream() -> Base64InputStream -> TarArchiveInputStream (131-132) -> loop archive.getNextEntry() (133-135) -> File f = new File(destination.toFile(), entry.getName()) (140) -> directory case f.mkdirs() (141-144), file case parent.mkdirs() (146-149) -> new FileOutputStream(f) + ByteStreams.copy(archive, fs) (150-153). No call to Path.normalize()/getCanonicalPath(), no startsWith(destination) check, and no name sanitization anywhere in the class. Contrast Copy.java:198, where the same class deliberately uses destPath.getFileName() when creating an outgoing tar entry: the incoming path is the untrusted one.
candidates.unverified: Not runtime-confirmed (no code execution and no cluster): I did not exercise extraction with a crafted archive, and I did not verify which application call sites copy from untrusted pods. The JVM's effective file-write permissions and any outer sandbox wrapping the client bound the impact, and some callers may legitimately treat the copied-from pod as fully trusted.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-22 Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal') / archive extraction (Zip Slip)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 1,730 source-root files; 1,724 model-visible, with 6 files excluded by the harness sensitive-name/path filter (the util/.../credentials/ classes referenced by ClientBuilder are present in imports but read_file rejects them). Binary-like files are skipped by policy and per-file text is capped at 5 MiB. Relation index: partial - 1,721/1,730 files indexed, 954 Java files parsed, 9 source files missing from the index, 5 omitted; it provides only syntax containment plus name/type/arity-based call and inheritance candidates, with control flow, data flow, semantic resolution and reachability explicitly not implemented, no SAST oracle loaded, and Spring support limited to annotation-name candidates. I reviewed the hand-written (non-generated) surface: util (KubeConfig, ClientBuilder, Config, SSLUtils, Yaml, Copy, Exec, Attach, PortForward, PodLogs, ProtoClient, Watch, WebSockets, WebSocketStreamHandler, authenticators, generic API, labels/accessors, informer core), extended (leader election and locks, events, workqueue, controllers, pager, kubectl), the spring processors, and the openapi core (ApiClient, JSON, auth classes, Configuration, custom types), and searched generated API/model files for missing parameter escaping (all path substitutions checked were escaped).
limitations: The six files under util/src/main/java/io/kubernetes/client/util/credentials/ are excluded from the model-visible view (both B0 and P1); ClientCertificateAuthentication/KubeconfigAuthentication logic could not be inspected, so any issue there is uncovered.
No code was executed and no cluster was contacted; the Copy finding is a source-level lead, not a runtime-confirmed exploit.
The ~750 generated openapi API/model files and large proto classes were only spot-checked (I verified path-parameter escaping patterns and a few auth/SSL/JSON paths), not read exhaustively.
Parts of the informer implementation (DeltaFIFO remainder, Cache, DefaultSharedIndexInformer, SharedInformerFactory) and examples/docs were not read in full.

The relation index has no data-flow/reachability analysis, so precedence/usage facts derived from it (for example who calls Copy) are navigation hints only and were verified against source where used.
Whether a given application copies directories from untrusted pods is application-dependent; the candidate's severity depends on that usage.

rejected_leads.lead: Unsafe SnakeYAML deserialization in io.kubernetes.client.util.Yaml: CustomConstructor extends org.yaml.snakeyaml.constructor.Constructor (util/src/main/java/io/kubernetes/client/util/Yaml.java:323) wired in getSnakeYaml() (lines 464-466), with snakeyaml 1.26 pinned in pom.xml; loading untrusted YAML with '!!' tags can instantiate arbitrary classes (CWE-502, CVE-2022-1471 class of issue).
rejected_leads.reason: Real weakness pattern but weaker as the primary finding: no in-repo production code feeds untrusted YAML to this utility (only examples/YamlExample.java uses it), and the project's own config parser deliberately uses SafeConstructor (KubeConfig.java:83), so this is arguably a hardening gap rather than a reachable defect in this snapshot. Kept as the strongest secondary lead.

rejected_leads.lead: Command injection via srcPath in Copy.copyFileFromPod (Copy.java:79) and Copy.copyDirectoryFromPod (Copy.java:127): sh -c "cat " + srcPath + " | base64" and "tar cz - " + srcPath + " | base64".
rejected_leads.reason: srcPath is chosen by the calling application rather than by a remote party, so normally no privilege boundary is crossed (and execution happens inside a container the caller can already exec into). Same file as the submitted candidate but a distinct, weaker root cause.

rejected_leads.lead: FilePersister.save rewrites the kubeconfig (including refreshed OIDC/GCP tokens) with new FileWriter(configFile) without restricting file permissions (FilePersister.java:51-56).
rejected_leads.reason: Requires a local attacker on the same host and a pre-existing permissive file/umask; no source-visible remote boundary; lower impact than the submitted candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: Request path/query construction without encoding in Exec.ExecutionBuilder.makePath (Exec.java:281-296) and Attach.ConnectionBuilder.makePath (Attach.java:212-226).
rejected_leads.reason: Namespace/name/container are supplied by the calling application (server-side code), not attacker-controlled in the normal flow; low, mostly correctness-level impact.

rejected_leads.lead: Self-recursive equals()/hashCode() in EventAggregator.AggregatedRecord (extended/src/main/java/io/kubernetes/client/extended/event/legacy/EventAggregator.java:95-103) could cause infinite recursion/StackOverflowError.
rejected_leads.reason: The class is private and its equals/hashCode are not invoked anywhere in the repository (Guava cache values are not compared), so there is no attacker-reachable path and no concrete security impact in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: TLS verification can be disabled in ApiClient.applySslSettings (kubernetes/.../ApiClient.java:1289-1315), and OIDC refresh sends the refresh token to the token_endpoint taken from the issuer's .well-known document (OpenIDConnectAuthenticator.java:191-291).
rejected_leads.reason: The trust-all TrustManager/hostname verifier is gated on verifyingSsl=false, which is only set from the kubeconfig opt-in insecure-skip-tls-verify (KubeConfig.verifySSL / ClientBuilder), i.e. intentional documented behavior; the OIDC issuer is kubeconfig-controlled, so no remote attacker controls it. Reported as counterevidence/context, not as candidates.

summary: Snapshot is kubernetes-client/java, pom version 9.0.1 (openapi-codegen output dated 2020-06), modules kubernetes/util/proto/extended/spring/examples, no test sources present. I reviewed the hand-written (non-generated) surface end to end and spot-checked generated API/model code for escaping anomalies (none found). The strongest source-evidenced issue is in io.kubernetes.client.Copy.copyDirectoryFromPod: the tar stream is produced by executing tar inside the target container (sh -c "tar cz - <srcPath> | base64"), and every TarArchiveEntry.getName() is used verbatim as a relative path under the caller's destination (new File(destination.toFile(), entry.getName())) with no normalization/containment check before mkdirs()/FileOutputStream, so a malicious or compromised container can return entries such as ../../... and write arbitrary files on the machine running the client (CWE-22 / archive Zip Slip; the same class as kubectl cp CVE-2019-11246/11249, whose fix was exactly this client-side validation, absent here). The closest competing lead is the unsafe SnakeYAML Constructor used by the library's Yaml utility (CWE-502), kept as a rejected lead because it requires an application to pass untrusted YAML to that optional helper and no in-repo production caller does, while the project's own config parser deliberately uses SafeConstructor.
